claims.text: A nanostructured, compositionally graded self-lubricating coating on CoCrFeNi will form an adaptive tribolayer during sliding.
The coating will maintain low friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
Low friction and wear will be maintained regardless of varying load and environmental conditions.
The starting material is an unmodified CoCrFeNi HEA that may be produced by laser additive manufacturing.
A nanostructured coating with a compositional gradient can dynamically promote tribolayer formation.
The adaptive tribolayer will consist of nanocrystalline or amorphous phases.
The tribolayer will adjust its structure in response to temperature and contact stress.
Sliding will cause the coating to release lubricious species or undergo in situ compositional changes.
The released species or compositional changes will form a protective tribolayer.
The protective tribolayer will reduce effective interfacial shear strength.
The tribolayer will counteract oxidation and wear.
Adaptation to thermal and mechanical loading will maintain consistently low friction and wear.
Relative to uncoated CoCrFeNi, the coated material will have a significantly lower steady-state coefficient of friction throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
Relative to uncoated CoCrFeNi, the coated material will have a significantly lower wear rate throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi has temperature-dependent friction and wear performance that deteriorates because protective films form inconsistently and oxidation varies with load and atmosphere.
The intervention is effective from room temperature to 800 °C under typical tribological sliding loads.
Loads or reactive species beyond typical operating conditions may limit coating performance.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims effectiveness regardless of load and environmental conditions, whereas the boundary states that excessive loads or reactive species may limit performance.
